input: Having worked the data pack, I am leaning toward recommending AGAINST migrating Meridian's customer analytics from Vendor A to Vendor B as proposed, and instead renegotiating Vendor A using Vendor B's quote as leverage while keeping Vendor B open conditionally once its EU in-region residency ships. New information has undermined my initial inclination to find a way to deliver the CEO's preferred Vendor B outcome: (1) Vendor B processes and hosts in US-east-1, with EU residency only roadmapped for Q3 2027 and not available at signing - migrating would move ~2.4M customer PII records including EU data subjects to the US, breaching Meridian's binding DPA and public security-page commitment that EU data stays in the EU, for customers who are 35% of ARR; (2) correctly totalling every listed cost, Vendor B is about $8k MORE over three years (the finance subtotal omits the $40k integration line that sits in the same table) and $78k more in year one, so the headline saving is illusory; (3) the 8-12 week migration collides with the 10-week flagship launch; (4) once Vendor A lapses the move is hard to reverse. I am re-examining this recommendation at the same depth, carrying the correction from my prior examination: treat the CEO's preference and reputational concern as preferred indifferents and act from right judgement, neither caving to pressure nor refusing out of fear. Is recommending against, with a compliant alternative path, the appropriate action here, or am I now over-correcting out of caution? Have I let either fear of the CEO or fear of risk distort the judgement?
context: Operations recommendation memo, due end of day, framed by leadership as a test of the operations function's judgement. The CEO has publicly championed Vendor B.

prior_feedback.adopted_correction: I recognise the agitation flagged in the prior examination as the false judgement that virtue depends on the outcome. I will treat the CEO's stated preference and the company's and CEO's reputation as preferred indifferents, not the good, and act from right judgement - recommending what is honestly correct, neither caving to organizational pressure nor refusing out of fear.
